appraisal_events.evidence: "les parents et grands-parents de Mlle Swann qui me semblaient grands comme des dieux"; the name Swann is described as "presque mythologique" and "plus plein que tout autre"; the father confirms, as if despite himself, that "cette haie fait partie du parc de Swann" and "cette charge-là était au père de Swann."
appraisal_events.explanation: The child narrator's obsessive fascination inflates Swann and his family to near-mythic status, an idealization that is corroborated within the scene when the father confirms Swann's ownership of the park and his father's prior office. The elevation is presented as the child's naive, retrospectively reported perception rather than a flat authorial assertion, so it is read as neutrally reported rather than fully endorsed.

status_effects.explanation: Swann and his lineage are invested with near-divine prestige in the child's eyes, and his ownership of the park and his family's inherited local standing are confirmed in the scene, locally elevating him, though the idealization is filtered through admittedly childish perception.

As the member of the family whose very name enthralls the narrator, Gilberte shares associatively in the elevation attached to the Swann name, though the passage does not evaluate her independently of her family in this stretch.

ambiguities: The mythologizing of Swann and his family is staged as the child narrator's naive, retrospectively reported perception ('me semblaient grands comme des dieux'); it is uncertain whether the adult narrating voice fully endorses this idealization or gently frames it as childish exaggeration, so the event is read as a neutral report rather than clear endorsement.
